utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Now preliminary matters raised by the parties, but I have a few matters I'd like to deal with in order to shorten my -- the Chamber's agenda. The first one deals with an issue remaining from the testimony of Vladimir Radojcic. On the 15th of December of last year, the Prosecution brought to the Chamber's attention through an e-mail that Exhibit P6955 - that is, 65 ter 1D2153 - was also admitted with a different ERN as Exhibit P4424. The Chamber notes that the two translations do not correspond. On the 16th and the 17th of December, the Chamber e-mailed the Defence to inquire if it had any objections to vacating Exhibit P6955 as suggested by the Prosecution, but as of today's date, the Defence has not responded. Is the Defence now able to advise the Chamber of its position with regard to Exhibits P6955 and P4424? That is a question. If not, I'll give you a relatively short deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. A short deadline would suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to mark P6955 as not admitted, and -- no, no. We'll leave that what -- First of all, we'd like to hear from the Defence by next Monday close of business, and we'll then proceed having heard from the Defence. The next item I'd like to deal with is the remaining issue from the testimony of Milorad Bukva. As a matter of fact there are even issues, the plural. On the 8th of September of last year the Chamber e-mailed the Prosecution inquiring whether it required a translation of the manuscript portions of Exhibit D613, which is a map admitted during the testimony of Witness Milorad Bukva. You could check on transcript pages 25037 to -038. And on the 29th of October, the Prosecution advised the Chamber that the translation of the manuscript comments would be welcome. However, the Prosecution also submitted that military maps from both the ABiH and the VRS were already in evidence and served as better evidence. The Prosecution also noted in its e-mail of the 29th of October and at transcript page 26098 that the Chamber may be assisted in understanding symbols made by witnesses on non-military maps by referring to 65 ter 30651, which is a 93-page JNA manual entitled: Instructions on working maps in the armed forces. On the 25th of November and the 9th of December, the Chamber e-mailed the parties to inquire whether either party was in receipt of a revised translation of D613. On the 10th of December, the Prosecution advised the Chamber that it was not in receipt of a revised translation; and on the 16th and the 17th of December, the Chamber e-mailed the Defence again to inquire whether it had an update with regard to the revised translation of D613 and whether it had any objections to the admission of 65 ter 30651; that is, the manual I just referred to. As of today's date, the Defence has not responded to the Chamber. The question is whether the Chamber can receive a response now and if not we'll set a deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not one I'm working on, but I think a short deadline should suffice and I'll make sure it gets done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber would like to hear by next Monday whether there is a revised translation of D613 and whether the Defence objects to the admission of 65 ter 30651. Then I have two matters I'd like to deal with in private session. Can we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will deliver a decision and perhaps meanwhile the usher could already start preparing the witness for entering the courtroom. We'll deliver now the decision on the admission into evidence of the witness statement and associated exhibits for Witness Mihajlo Vujasin. On the 7th of August of last year, the Defence filed a motion to tender the witness statement together with 31 associated exhibits. On the 21st of August, the Prosecution reserved its position on the admissions of statement and associated exhibits as the documents had not been disclosed properly. On 16th of December the Chamber invited the Defence to reduce the number of associated exhibits tendered with this witness. The Defence subsequently provided a reduced list of associated exhibits tendering eight of 31 exhibits. Of the remaining exhibits, the document bearing 65 ter 1D04082 was admitted into evidence as Exhibit D642; thereby, leaving seven associated exhibits and the witness's statement, which was MFI'd as Exhibit D641. The Prosecution indicated that it did not object to the admission of these seven associated exhibits which can be found on pages 25595 to 25601.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I ask for some patience. I will continue to read a decision and we'll then continue with your testimony. I continue reading the decision. The Chamber recalls that the case law with regard to the admission of associated exhibits pursuant to Rule 92 ter establishes that documents can be admitted if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written testimony. And with regard to the admission of the witness statement, the Chamber recalls Rules 89(C) and Rule 92 ter. The Chamber has reviewed the witness statement and the proposed associated exhibits. The Chamber considers the witness statement to be relevant to the indictment, Schedules F and G, and was attested to by the witness. It therefore finds it to be relevant and of probative value for the purpose of admission pursuant to Rules 89(C) and 92 ter. The Chamber hereby admits the witness statement as it was MFI'd previously as D641. It's hereby admitted into evidence. With regard to the exhibits bearing document numbers 1D03109, 1D03110, and 1D04095, these exhibits consist of maps marked by the witness which give further explanation to paragraphs 4 and 22 of the statement. The Chamber considers that the statement would be thus less comprehensible without them. With regard to the exhibit bearing number 1D04096, this document was used during the witness's testimony to further explain paragraph 61 of the witness statement; in particular, what was meant by "unrealistic expectations of the brigade." And this can be found on transcript pages 25591 to -594. The statement would thus be less comprehensible without it. With regard to exhibits bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 08346, 1D04093, and 1D04094, these exhibits are only mentioned in the statement but do not contribute to the content or the comprehensibility of the statement and additionally were not discussed in the court by the witness. The Chamber hereby admits the documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 1D03109, 1D03110, 1D04095, and 1D04096. Madam Registrar, four numbers for these documents in the order as I read them out would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives exhibit number D872, D873, D874, and D875, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D872 up to and including D875 are admitted into evidence. The Chamber denies admission of the documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 08346, 1D04093, and 1D04094. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of Witness Mihajlo Vujasin's statement and associated exhibits. Mr. Kevac, we asked a lot of your patience; apologies for that. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Ms. Edgerton will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to continue on a topic that we finished off with yesterday, and it's the topic of resubordination of police units. Now -- to the military. And now at transcript page 30498, you told His Honour Judge Orie, and I'll quote that: "On a tactical level, it wasn't possible to carry out resubordination of police units to the commander of the tactical level. The commander of a tactical level who is an officer who was a division commander or lower than that." Now, that's what you said yesterday by way of a little reminder for you, and I'd like to, in relation to that, show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 31827.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is a -- this is a short document. It's an order dated 22 June 1992 from Colonel Galic to Operations Group 30, the 1st Infantry Brigade, and the 19th Partisan Brigade. But I'd like you to have a look at the order, and I want to draw your attention, in particular, to the last two paragraphs which say: "In exceptional cases where there is an urgent need, police forces may be used for direct combat activities on the front to hold and strengthen the front until the arrival of army units. "In other cases, it is necessary to inform and receive permission from the chief of the Security Services Centre." So, Mr. Kevac, this is Colonel Galic doing exactly what you told His Honour Judge Orie yesterday it was impossible to do, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, we're talking about exceptional situations when there is a threat or a danger that the area populated by the civilian population comes under threat from the enemy side. In that case, in order to defend the area, police units are also engaged in defence, pending the arrival of military units. Those were exceptional cases. There were no such cases in the area of responsibility of the division, so I can't say whether the police were engaged in keeping with this decision of the division commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're changing the evidence you gave His Honour Judge Orie yesterday where you said it was not possible to carry out the resubordination, aren't you, seeing this document that I've just shown you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This exceptional engagement of police units was certainly approved by the police minister. Police organs had the approval for such engagement in exceptional situations. This was regulated at the highest level. Brigade commanders could not use police units without approval issued by authorised bodies. Because, as it says under bullet point 1, the police are used to keep law and order. This is their duty, and that's how they are used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was, Mr. Kevac, whether you agreed that having seen this document, you're changing the evidence you gave yesterday. That's correct, isn't it, you're changing the evidence you gave yesterday, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not changing my evidence. I just confirmed that at the tactical level the commander could not use the police; i.e., the term "resubordination" is a term which I don't know how you interpret. Resubordination means that if a unit is assigned to a commander, he can uses it up to a certain point in time. After then, that unit is resubordinated to another commander and that other commander continues using it for a different task. Resubordination means that a unit is placed from one command to another command, from the command by one commander to the command of another commander. This document doesn't specify very clear whether we're talking about resubordination or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. We have the document now. We have the testimony of the witness of yesterday. We have the testimony of the witness of today. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just have the document as a Prosecution exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- before we go further please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31872 [sic] receives exhibit number P7051, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also yesterday you said that with respect to the Velagici killings you heard there were proceedings initiated against the perpetrators. And my first question to you on that point is: When you talk about what happened in Velagici, you mean the killing on June 1st, 1992, of at least 77 men who had been detained at the school house in Velagici by members of the VRS. That's what you mean; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the details of that case. I did not have an occasion to see the reports issued by the police bodies that carried out the on-site inspection and continued to process the whole event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, if I may just interrupt before you proceed. When you introduced P8051, at page 9, line 8 -- or 8, line 9, sorry. Yeah, at 8 -- line 8. It was introduced as 31827. When it is admitted at line 10 -- at page 10, line 11, it is 31872. Which is the correct one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 31827, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 2-7. It's not your mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby then corrected. Witness, in relation to the last question, you may not know the details, but when you said that proceedings were instituted against suspects, you were dealing with the killing of a large number of men that had been detained at the Velagici school. Is that what you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- and that's what you talked about when you said that proceedings were instituted against suspects. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you know those suspects were never prosecuted, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, and I don't know how the proceedings ended against those suspects, because that was not in my remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, also yesterday at transcript pages 30493 to 30494 you talked about the events of the 28th May 1992 as being a response -- actually you said: "In this particular case, this was just a response to the Muslim activity against the JNA column." And then further you said: "In other words, those activities were carried out as a counter-measure after the Muslim forces had attacked the column." Now, in fact, Mr. Kevac, the action -- pardon me. The -- the -- this wasn't -- this action wasn't a counter-measure at all and your consistent reference to the attack on the JNA column is nothing more than a pretext, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at this for a minute. What happened on the 27th of May was isolated incidents in local Muslim-held pockets in a larger Serb-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd refer Your Honours to P3851 and P2867 in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if she's relying upon exhibits, in questioning the witness she needs to present them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton has asked a question to the witness and has informed the Chamber that relevant information could be found by the Chamber in those documents, but she doesn't put those documents to the witness. She puts a question to the witness. Perhaps at a later stage she'll confront the witness with the documents, but she started by just putting that question. Would you please answer that question: Whether what happened were isolated incidents in local Muslim-held pockets in a larger Serb-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the entire Kljuc area municipality was a quiet area. The entire area was such that Serb and Muslim populations lived there peacefully. There was no defined space controlled either by Serbs or Muslims. It was all common space. And, at that time, Mr. Omer Filipovic was the vice-president of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. He participated in the authority, in the running of the Kljuc municipality. So I don't know of any areas that were under the control of Muslims or areas that were under the control of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your response to these isolated incidents and the failure to disarm was to launch attacks, widespread attacks, against the locations that we've seen in the documents yesterday and areas of the municipality, including by shelling those areas; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In those attacks on those Muslim-held areas, civilians were killed. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that an order was issued for an attack or that the army had the task of executing an attack. The army, Colonel Galic, in a direct conversation with Mr. Filipovic, requested that the Muslims hand over their weapons. When they failed to do that, Colonel Galic ordered that a volley be fired as a warning in the direction of the place where the ambush was. I said yesterday that I don't know where the shells actually fell or if there were any casualties as a consequence of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, the question didn't relate to an order to attack; it related to the attack. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An order is required for every assignment that is being carried out. In this case, it was the action of disarming Muslim paramilitaries in the municipal territory of Kljuc. It was conducted in such a way that there was a search carried out, looking for weapons and armed persons in the territory of the municipality. This is not a form of action that could be described as an attack. An attack is an assault on entrenched positions of the enemy in order to inflict losses on the enemy using weapons and in order to capture their positions. That's an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm happy that you deny that this was an attack. There's a difference [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you also deny that civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any data about civilians being killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question wasn't, Mr. Kevac, whether or not you had data. My question was whether you denied that civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not denying it. Probably they were killed, but I don't know anything about it. I didn't have information about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's also correct, isn't it, that during these operations we're discussing, that houses, private houses in Pudin Han, Velagici, these locations we're talking about, Biljani, Sanica, Prhovo, Muslim-held locations were burned; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely but I did hear of individual instances of some houses being torched. I wasn't in the area, but probably there were some houses that were burned. There were houses that were not burned also.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And non-Serbs were surrendering to VRS forces in the face of these operations en masse; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population in that area responded to calls to come out to hand over their weapons, those who had them. Those who didn't have weapons still came out to identify themselves to be there. A number of people fled. They were hiding in the woods, and there were armed Muslims in that area until late 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was about whether non-Serbs were surrendering to VRS forces. Now, you have described a lot of things but you didn't touch upon whether non-Serbs surrendered to VRS forces. Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the procedure that the units applied, the units that were searching the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were non-Serbs surrendering to the VRS forces irrespective of what specific procedure was applied? If you don't know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an area mostly populated by Muslims. Probably that's how it was. I don't know. I'm not able to confirm whether they were surrendering or whether they had just responded to the call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you don't know. Please be aware that you have -- you know a lot of details about what happened. You explained to us they came out, some of them with weapons, some of them without weapons. You know all the details. And if it comes to whether they surrendered to VRS forces, you don't know, which may raise questions as whether you are selective in your recollection because you give all the other details at this question. But if you don't know, that's fine. Then we'll move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just say this: The commander requested the Muslims to surrender their weapons. They surrendered their weapons and in that context they were surrendering too. That's how it was, in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, so they were surrendering. Why didn't you say five questions earlier, yes, they surrendered? Was -- that was the question. So they did surrender. The question was, in addition to that, did they surrender en masse. Was it a large number that surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with the population numbers in a certain place and the number of men, they would respond to the call to surrender, to hand over their weapons, I don't know if this disarming process was something that was en masse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you know all the details, you know that they surrendered, but whether there are many or not, you do not know. Fine. If you don't know, we'll move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you don't know that in your own division's area of responsibility people were surrendering to your forces en masse. So do you know that, in fact, across three municipalities at this time - Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor - non-Serbs were being captured by VRS forces by the thousands; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the area of responsibility of the 30th Division encompassed Kupres, Donji Vakuf, Turbe, Jajce, going all the way towards the confluence of the Ugar river into the Vrbas river. This is the position that was held by the division. Within that area, there was -- there was sections where there was no combat. The town of Kljuc, as such, was not part of the division's area of defence. Sanski Most and Prijedor, in particular, is where I heard that there was disarming of Muslims. In Sanski Most and Prijedor. I did hear of that. But I don't know of any details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, you've described your area of responsibility, which is fine, because then we know how you understand the question. Then you said a lot of things, including that there was disarming, but you have not given an answer to the question: Were you aware that non-Serbs were captured by the VRS forces by the thousands in your area of responsibility? Were you aware or were you not aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware that the terrain was being searched and that disarming was under way, and I did hear that a number of Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I stop you. I stop you. Why first answer questions which were not put to you. Were you aware that by the thousands non-Serbs were captured in that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're the ops officer for your division, and you've already explained how the reports you received from the division subordinate units would be sent up to the division commander and how his reports would then go up to General Talic, and in the normal course of things they'd reach the Main Staff. So if you don't know that the VRS in your area of responsibility was taking control of thousands of non-Serb detainees, how come General Talic knows while it's happening?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered yesterday that Muslims in the area of Kljuc were handed over to the civilian police and then transported further, according to their plan. This was not something that was done by the division units, so I cannot really talk about things that I don't know and what I didn't read in the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, the Muslims posed no real danger to VRS forces whatsoever, didn't they? You took control of the area of Kljuc within two days of those attacks. You know that, don't you, because you were the operations guy, and you were receiving all those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's five questions in one there, Ms. Edgerton. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I break them up please, Your Honour, then. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I -- I even encourage you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, the Muslim forces or the Muslims posed no real danger to you whatsoever; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the -- in the composite version of your questions, it was Muslims; now it is Muslim forces. So you are putting a different question to the witness. I don't know whether he is sufficiently -- was sufficiently aware of the first version of your question and the second one. You see that your language is not the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you took control of the area of Kljuc within two days of those attacks; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attacks were not organised other than warning volleys after which Omer Filipovic announced that the Muslim Territorial Defence in the Kljuc area would surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it correct that VRS forces took control, full control of the area of Kljuc within two days of these isolated attacks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks as if there's some confusion. From the answer of the witness, I do understand that he thinks the question was about attacks by the Serbs, whereas the attacks you refer to, Ms. Edgerton, seem to be the isolated incidents of attack where Muslims attacked Serbs, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore the witness, in his answer, is apparently not understanding what attacks you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the incidents you've been talking about on the 27th of May, 1992. Now, is it correct that VRS forces took full control of the area of Kljuc municipality within two days of those attacks, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just have a look, please, at one more document and then we'll leave this area. It's P2875.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is a report to the 1st Krajina Corps Command from their morale and legal affairs officer. And I want you to have a look at the fourth full paragraph in both languages, actually, on page 1. It says, about the third sentence down -- actually, we can look at the beginning of the paragraph. It refers to the military column coming from Knin where two soldiers were killed, four were wounded. And then slightly further, it says: "Energetic action by our 30th Partisan Division resulted in the defeat and breakup of those forces in the town of Kljuc itself in the villages of Pudin Han, Velagici, Donji Ramici. Units of the corps have established full control of the area." It talks about weapons seized, and then says: "About 280 enemy soldiers were captured in Kljuc and a number of them killed." Once again, you're contradicted by a contemporaneous military document, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I find it in the structure that counsel has skipped over the part that says "and some enemy soldiers fled into the surrounding area." That, if you're being -- present a document to the witness to comment, you should have the full document, not picking parts of it to construct the view is in favour of the Prosecution's theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it really changes that much, but, Ms. Edgerton, it -- indeed, the document also describes that some of the enemy troops escaped, have escaped in the surrounding mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then let's then -- The question now to you is where you said there was no attack, it was just firing a few shells to warn, and then everyone handed in their weapons. Nothing was organised. Ms. Edgerton puts to you that the document gives a different picture from what you told us, and I take it invites you to comment on the contradiction between your testimony and what is found in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot clarify it other than to say that that this energetic action represents one volley representing the decisiveness of the army to resolve the situation in that area. As far as I see and as far as I know, there was no other action. After that, the action of disarming of military Muslim formations was carried out in that area. The report refers to three villages: Pudin Han, Velagici, and Donji Ramici. This is not the whole of the Kljuc municipality. Other than these villages, there are many other villages where Muslims lived and where there was no disarmament action or a sweeping of the terrain in search of hidden weapons, and this is what my answer referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see it's time just about for the first break of the morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and I think you have approximately some -- you used 35 minutes approximately so you've 25 minutes left. Well, that's for two hours, because yesterday you used one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. I hope to be done well within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, you may follow the usher. We take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, the sheer scale of what the VRS did in response to these isolated incidents in the three villages you just spoke about before we broke shows that the operation against the Muslims was far more than a counter-measure. In fact, it was a co-ordinated and planned operation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it was designed -- it was all about pushing the non-Serbs out of Kljuc; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we'll just move on to a related area, actually. You said that -- in your written evidence at paragraph 17, which is on page 5 in English, you said the safety of the Muslims in Kljuc was guaranteed. And then yesterday at transcript page 30460, you were asked: "Who was tasked with this protection of the population?" And your answer was: "The MUP or the civilian police was in charge of that." But, in fact, the VRS and the police were together committing massive crimes against the non-Serbs in Kljuc, weren't they, Mr. Kevac?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it misstates the evidence. I believe the testimony that is being referred to refers to paragraph 16 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, were you referring to paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was specifically referring to the sentence in paragraph 17 that says: "No one touched them and their safety was guaranteed." And I quoted the line from the testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, apparently Mr. Ivetic understood it in a different way. It's now clear what Ms. Edgerton referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, the transcript referred to paragraph 16, that's my point. The question is being -- the answer is being cited as in relation to paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's yesterday's transcript, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. I have the page open now, 30460. My question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me a second --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then I have it open.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Line 13 through the end of the page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question yesterday, Ms. Edgerton, was related to what you read yesterday from paragraph 16, so the testimony is to be understood as in response to a question in which you read out paragraph 16 and that is not exactly the same lines as you are apparently referring to now in paragraph 17. So perhaps you should make this as clear as possible by either -- perhaps by quoting both the testimony and the line you wanted to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I wanted to remind the witness initially of his written evidence which says, at paragraph 17: "The Muslims that lived in Kljuc lived there peacefully. No one touched them and their safety was guaranteed." And, then, separately, I chose at the same time to remind the witness of his testimony which was in answer to a question by Mr. Ivetic, actually, yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made a mistake there. It was Mr. Ivetic who then referred to paragraph 16, and the witness then answered that. Sorry to interrupt to you, but I made a mistake, indeed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, not at all, Your Honours. But now -- your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Kevac, was: The VRS and the police were together committing massive crimes against the non-Serbs in Kljuc, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about crimes committed by individuals in the territory of Kljuc municipality. They were committed by individuals and proceedings were instituted against them. This is as much as I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if -- there apparently is an issue about whether these were isolated individuals just acting on their own or whether these were members of police forces or military forces. First question: When you talk about individuals, do you mean to say individuals that were not in any way members of police forces or military forces? Is that what you intend to refer to, if you say "individuals"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my statement, I stated that I'd heard about members of the Army of Republika Srpska who committed a crime in the school, in Velagici. I also heard that the military police had carried out an on-site investigation and that those soldiers were arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, again, you apparently consider it very important to tell us again and again that they were arrested. But I then understand if you're talking about "individuals," of course, crimes are often committed by persons. Now those individuals, if I understand your testimony now well, that they may well have been members of the police force or the military forces. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stated that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness -- Mr. Ivetic is on his feet and the witness seems to be waiting for Mr. Ivetic to say something, so perhaps we could resolve that before the witness continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let the witness answer and then I'll make my point for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, if I put a question to you -- just look at me; to no one else. I also noticed that you are seeking eye contact with Mr. -- at least the Defence side. I didn't know whom exactly you tried to reach. I repeat my question: Do I understand your testimony well that those individuals you're talking about may well have been members of the police or the military forces? The Serb police or military forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, Your Honour, for purposes of the record, the witness said precisely that at page 25, lines 1, just before Your Honour's question. So Your Honour's question was asking something that the witness had already answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ivetic. Again -- but I'm not entering into debates with you again and again. Earlier the witness was repeatedly referring to individuals, not specifically about the Velagici school but about all kind of incidents, this was what happened, and I wanted to clarify apart from the Velagici school whether when he refers to individuals, whether that could refer well to members of the police and the military forces. So, therefore, I'm afraid that either you didn't fully understand my question or you have not carefully looked at the answer the witness gave which was exclusively about Velagici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I draw Mr. Ivetic's attention to page 24, line 15 to 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, can you identify for us one single case where members of the VRS were prosecuted for committing war crimes against non-Serbs in Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that persons who committed the crime in Velagici were arrested and taken to the court in Banja Luka. What happened next, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, so therefore the answer is: I don't know whether they were prosecuted. So, indeed, as a matter of fact, the answer to the question is simply no, because you cannot identify one single case in which persons were prosecuted, and that they were arrested you have told us already many times. Ms. Edgerton please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Kevac? You can't identify one single war crimes prosecution where members of the VRS were prosecuted for committing war crimes against non-Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you about any single case that was brought to an end, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Similarly, can you identify for us one single case where members of the VRS were prosecuted for killing non-Serbs in Kljuc municipality? A murder charge.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information. I don't know whether anybody was charged and found guilty of murder.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, isn't this a matter which -- I mean, if there would have been prosecutions for crimes committed in Kljuc, why not agree on that? Whether this witness knows about it is a different matter. I would urge the parties to seek an agreement on that. If no one was ever prosecuted, then ... that isn't too difficult to agree upon, I would think, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now we'll go back to my first question that began this discussion. And the question was whether you would agree that -- in fact, I'll read it to you. I asked you whether the police and the VRS together were committing massive crimes against the non-Serbs in Kljuc. Now, in fact, what they were doing, Mr. Kevac, was that they were burning homes, they were looting property, and they were arbitrarily arresting people. That's what was going on in Kljuc. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the territory of Kljuc municipality, Muslim formations were disarmed in an operation that was carried out. There were casualties, and houses were indeed torched during that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so, in fact, the people whose job it was to protect the civilians against these massive crimes were themselves the perpetrators; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about civilians, we're talking about unarmed persons. In this particular case, those people had weapons and used those weapons against the JNA column and against members of the Kljuc police, and that resulted in people being killed and wounded. The operation to disarm those armed individuals was carried out after their commander, Omer Filipovic, announced that they were prepared to surrender. Civilians, i.e., women, children, and elderly persons, were not subject of searches, and they were not brought in by the police as a result of that -- that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I would have a few questions if you would allow me. You said a minute ago, Witness, you said -- let me find it to quote you literally. You talked about Muslim formations being disarmed, an operation was carried out, "there were casualties, and houses were indeed torched during that operation." Do I have to understand this as that those who were involved in this operation were involved in the torching of houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know who torched houses, whether those were military or somebody else who arrived after the military had departed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you don't know. You were not present at the time. Is that why you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then tell us how you knew that only those who had weapons were detained? How do you know that if you were not present at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that from the division commander when he arrived at the division command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he tell you approximately how many people had weapons and how many did not have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About how many people had weapons and how many didn't, he did not give me the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but, proportions? 70 per cent had weapons or 300 had weapons, something of the kind, even without exact numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that a large quantity of weapons was confiscated. I didn't hear exact numbers. I don't remember that an exact number was ever mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How are you sure that those who had no weapons were not detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that those who had no weapons were not innate. Those who were brought in were processed. And based on the information on who was a member of the Territorial Defence and who wasn't, those people who were brought in were grouped into categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what happened to the category that had no weapons, well, let's say, men of military age, no weapons found on them. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, then you can't exclude any possibility, I take it, whether they continued to be detained or were released. You don't know? Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kevac, you made the point that the women and the children and the elderly were not -- in Kljuc were not the subject of searches. But, Mr. Kevac, the women, the children, the elderly who hadn't been arrested had absolutely no guarantees of safety; right? Because the authorities were the ones who were perpetrating the crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you please -- you are inviting the witness to say something and then also to give the reasons for what he should confirm or not. That is really complex. Ask questions please --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- about facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, you made the point that the women, the children, and the elderly weren't the subject of searches. These were the same people who -- whose male family members had been arrested in large numbers; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They had, the non-Serb women, children, and elderly, had no guarantees of security, in fact; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question because I was not a member of the authorities who were supposed to provide them with security. I'm talking about the civilian police and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's stick, then, to facts. You say houses were torched. Now the question put to you by Ms. Edgerton is a rather abstract one, but if your house is torched, then at least no security was given such as to prevent the house being torched. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So these people left Kljuc, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some did. Some of those people left Kljuc. Some remained living in Kljuc, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And they left because of the climate of fear, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation. The witness can't be asked to testify about the mental state and reasons of third parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that similar questions have not been put to witnesses at various times. But I would agree. Let's first try to stick to facts, Ms. Edgerton. To that extent I grant the objection made. Previous question, you said: Those people left. You said some left. Some remained. How many left; how many remained? If you don't have exact numbers, I understand, but in proportions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have exact numbers. However, over one half certainly left. I don't know how many more than one half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But more than one half. Could it have been 95 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. It was probably less than 95 per cent, but I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the basis at all that you know that it was more than 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because it was something that happened on a substantial scale. They requested to leave Kljuc. The authorities allowed that to happen. I heard about it. I wasn't present. I happened to be in a different place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't have any personal knowledge about it of personal observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you talk to those persons before they left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I was at the division command. I was not in the Kljuc municipality area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge - and on what basis - about the reasons why they left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say. I think that their main reason for leaving was because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what you think. Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was war time. Everyone was afraid, Serbs, Muslims. Everyone was afraid for the survival of their families. Everybody wanted to place their families in a place where they felt that they would be safer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is true for Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. Some Serb families left Kljuc municipality to go to Serbia, to go abroad, because they felt unsafe because of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, was that also more than 50 per cent, that Serbs, the percentage, that left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were fewer than 50 per cent of Serbs, so it was a smaller percentage of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What approximately? How many families is it in your recollection that left for safety purposes, Serb families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot say exactly how many there were. All I know is that they left the Kljuc municipality area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for exact number. Is it ten families, is it 500 families, is it -- approximately, if you know? If you say I've got no idea how many left, then please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know the exact number. All I know is that they were leaving the territory of Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You apparently ignored that I said that you didn't have to give exact figures. But, please, Ms. Edgerton proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your priority wasn't about protecting the Muslims from any of the crimes we've been discussing, was it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so. Members of the Army of Republika Srpska were told how they should conduct themselves, in what manner, and not to commit crimes against enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at one last document to wrap this up today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: P3769, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a report dated 16 February 1993 to the 1 KK Command from Slobodan Dakic, and it's about a meeting of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly and the situation in Kljuc from that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go over to page 2 in both languages, the second-to-last full paragraph, I think, from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It says with respect to the onset of the war --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's the last full paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the onset of the war in Kljuc municipality --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, we can start at the paragraph above.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to focus you on one sentence. It says: "The Serbian army, police and Serbian people crushed and routed genocide prone Ustashas in one fell swoop and cleansed the remaining Ustashas from Kljuc." And then says: "By this act, the Serbian people made a clean break once and for all with the centuries-old enemy." In the next paragraph, it says -- it talks about: "Individuals and small and large groups of people began illegally appropriating Muslim property in Muslim villages and hamlets during combat operations" in some of the area we've been discussing and continued to do so when operations ended. This was done by military personnel, members of the police, and local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now if we can go on to page three 3 both language. I think the fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. I have to find it on the page. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Those and other acts," referring to different crimes. "Those and other acts are being committed in full views of those who were supposed to stop and prevent them and this in full co-ordinated action and co-operation of civilian and military police." Mr. Kevac, these crimes were all about pushing the non-Serbs out of Kljuc municipality and provoking fear in those that remained. That's what this document shows. And, once again, my question is: You're contradicted by the contemporaneous evidence, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about anything like that. What I see now is that somebody has written something. I don't know who it was. The person who wrote it was not a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. So as far as these political decisions and events in the Kljuc municipal territory is concerned, I don't know what happened, what they discussed amongst themselves ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say the author was not a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. Do you know the author?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat what I said. I think it was Dakic. I think Dakic was a journalist in the Kljuc municipality area. As far as I know, he was not a member of the army. I don't know if he was or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you testified that he was not. You said he was not a member of the army, and now you tell us that you don't know. That -- you should be more cautious in not giving evidence where you, three seconds later, say you don't know. Apart from, I think, that Ms. Edgerton told you what his position was when she introduced the document, but let's leave it to that. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the fact is, the military and civilian police committing crimes with impunity against the Muslims in Kljuc removed any real choice they might have had about staying in their municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm whether this is so or not so. This person wrote that and he probably felt that was so. I already said that after the Muslim forces surrendered, the majority of Muslims left the municipality of Kljuc, and after that houses were burned individually, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, a minute ago you told us that you did not know whether the houses were torched during the operation or after the operation. Now you tell us that it was after the operation. Could you tell us what's the source of your knowledge that it did not happen during the operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I didn't know whether it was during the operation or after the operation. All I know is that houses were burned, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, a second ago, you said: "After the Muslims had left, houses were burned individually," which means after the operations. Isn't that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know for sure. I know that I did see burned-down houses. I don't know whether that was in the course of the cleansing operation or after the cleansing operation. That's something I cannot confirm. I assume that it happened then and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time in your testimony you say it happened afterwards, after you had half an hour ago told us that you don't know. I'm pointing at this because we noticed that you'll change your testimony sometimes easily even within a few minutes and you're here to tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And if you don't know anything, the whole truth is: I don't know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you were asked today by the Prosecutor -- actually, it was put to you by the Prosecutor that these Muslim forces in these villages did not pose a danger to you. How did the army view the attack on a radio repeater relay, the capturing the soldiers in one village, and the armed assault on a convoy of unarmed soldiers resulting in dozens of casualties?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army viewed that as a danger in relation to the army and the Serbian people in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I believe you mentioned in your testimony that there were other villages which were not searched for weapons that were inhabited by Muslims in Kljuc municipality. Had those villages inhabited by Muslims that were not searched, had they committed any assaults or attacks against the army in the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no incidents or attacks in those villages on members of the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go step by step through what would be expected in a standard mopping up operation per applicable JNA military doctrine. First of all, what would be expected for individuals who surrendered weapons, perhaps even legally owned weapons, and for whom the processing revealed they had not participated in combat activity or hostile activity. Now, what would happen to them after they were processed in a standard scenario?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we're interested in what happened not in standard scenarios.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Your Honour. I intend to use a document that Ms. Edgerton introduced yesterday that will show us what happened, and I want to see if that's in accord with what would be the standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Please answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A standard check of the weapons means checking if the weapons were not used in combat, the owner would receive his weapon back, and he would be informed about what the legal terms were for possessing and keeping weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the case that it was determined that he had not used his weapon in combat, what would the result be? Would that individual remain in someone's custody or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, the individual probably would not be kept any longer in detention because there would no evidence for keeping him in detention any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to go to a document that was used yesterday, because Your Honours want to see the situation in Kljuc at the time. And that is P3923; English page 59, B/C/S page 77. If we can go to the next page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the top of the page under -- in Serbian in results, at the bottom of the page in English, we see for this action the 29th of May in the villages of Pudin Han, Velagici, Donji Ramici, Sehici, the results say: "Arrested: 250 people who surrendered their weapons. After investigation, 100 were released to go home." Is this reporting from army organs reporting of a situation that you'd expect as standard in a legitimate mopping up operation per JNA doctrine?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at the next line: "About 1.000 refugees in the village of Ljusa: They were allowed to return home after a search of nearby villages." Is this action as reported in this military document in accord with the standard procedure for post-mopping up operation as understood under JNA doctrine?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- Mr. Ivetic, could I seek some clarification. The refugees in the village of Ljusa, where did they come from, what was their ethnicity, to the extent you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Ljusa is not in the Kljuc municipality area. I'm not sure, but it was inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But by Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly what that is. It says 1.000 refugees. They left their village and then they returned to their village. Refugee status, according to international rules, is something else. Here it was just a brief period when they left their village, they were in a different area, and then they returned to their villages. I don't know if they were actually refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge about what happened in Ljusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we go back to the prior page in B/C/S, and it is the third bullet point from the 30th pd in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "These areas will be difficult to hold because part of the forces fled to nearby mountains: An attack from these areas can be expected." Is this in accord with the information that you received subsequent to the actions in this area?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information was submitted to the division commander about a number of Muslim TO members handing over their weapons and a number not having handed over their weapons and that they escaped into the hills and the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to a different topic. Yesterday at transcript page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- since we are still on this page --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to have a few more questions. We just talked about the portion of this document, perhaps we move to the next page in B/C/S again, about the thousand refugees in Ljusa. The document also talks about: "Arrested: 250 people who surrendered their weapons. After investigation, 100 were released to go home." Do you have any personal knowledge of what happened and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any personal information or personal knowledge about what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether the 100 would have been elderly or military-aged men, you wouldn't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also would not know what kind of weapons were surrendered, whether these were legal or illegal weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday at transcript page 30496, 30498, and 30499, you were talking of something that was translated as joint action and co-ordinated action, but I believe the Serbian word you used was "sadejstvo." Could you please identify for us first is "sadejstvo" a recognised JNA combat doctrine?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the term sadejstvo, co-ordinated action, is defined in documents and rules of combat of the JNA, as well as in all combat documents and rules of all the armies. That term appears in all such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If an army unit is operating in "sadejstvo," or co-ordinated action, with a police units in the field, can the army commanding officer in the field issue orders to that police unit?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Co-ordinated action implies that two different units are carrying their own assignments and that each one is helping the other in executing their assignments. This is co-ordinated action. It does not imply the command authority of one unit over another unit; in this case, the command authority over the police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, also in the case of "sadejstvo," or co-ordinated action, between an army unit and a police unit in the field, to whom would those police units submit their post-action reports? Would it be to the army commander?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would submit reports to their own superior officer. Probably information would be exchanged with the other unit, the one that they were carrying out their co-ordinated action with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at transcript page 30498, lines 5 through 6 yesterday, you started to give an example from your own personal experience of when you operated together with a police unit in an area but you were not permitted to finish your answer and give this example. Could you please tell us about your personal experience of how a co-ordinated action was undertaken between your unit and a police unit which you started telling us about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a special police unit whose task was to go to a certain area and together with units from the 2nd Krajina Corps on the strength of the 3rd Petrovac Brigade, whose task was to be carried out on a condition that my brigade carried out its task. After a certain time they came to the corps command where I was, and they told us that their engagement period was over. It was a police unit. They were to return to their base irrespective of the fact that they did not manage to carry out the mission that they had been given by their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move to my last topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have three questions, Your Honours. I see we're close to the time for a break, but I have exactly three questions. So I leave it to your discretion whether you want to try to finish before or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we'd prefer to try to finish. I'm also looking at you, Ms. Edgerton. I don't know whether you'd need -- have any further questions as matters stand now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll try to conclude before we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday at transcript page 30471, lines 7 through 9, you were asked if the 17th Kljuc Brigade of the VRS was formed in April 1992. Do you know when the VRS itself was formed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS was established on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time that you were assigned for the first time to the 30th Partisan Division in May of 1992, did the Kljuc Light Infantry Brigade exist as a formation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When the Kljuc Light Infantry Brigade was formed in the beginning of June 1992, did the 30th Division continue to operate any units on the territory of the Kljuc municipality? And by "operate," I mean have command over.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR KEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not have a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thank you for the extra couple of minutes. That concludes my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I thank you for sticking very strictly to your three questions. The last question sometimes is the last of a series of questions, but you strictly adhered to that number, three. Have matters changed?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, this concludes your testimony before this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that you were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. We are calling Mr. Sabljic, Slavisa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to address the following matter. We -- the Chamber received on the 21st of January information from the Prosecution that the Prosecution will not -- as matters stand now, sees no reason to cross-examine the witness, and I think it's not a protected witness, Borislav Fejzovic, which means that the Chamber, taking matters step by step, does the same as it did (redacted), that is, to instruct the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That we take it step by step and that we will instruct the Defence to postpone calling this witness so that we can further consider the situation, and that will be until further notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way when I earlier said 21st of January I made a mistake, if that's what I said, because it was the 23rd of January. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for the Defence, for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sabljic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please slowly tell us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: Slavisa Sabljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljic, did you provide members of the Defence team of General Mladic a statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens 1D01748.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see a document on the screen. It is your statement in B/C/S, which is a reference to our language here at this Tribunal. Do you see a signature on this page and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to the last page in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see signatures on this page and do you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see them and I recognise them, of course. These are my signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to look at the statement. Would you say that everything that you stated before the General Mladic Defence team was properly recorded?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully and properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, as for the statement contents, is that correct and truthful, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: Yes, because this is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljic, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SABLJIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we would like to tender Mr. Sabljic's statement into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01748 receives Exhibit D876, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D876 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would, with your leave, just read a short -- actually summary statement of this witness and I will not have any questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please then read the summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As Judge Moloto reminded me, short summary statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
